lead: A PID controller turns the error between set point and output into a control signal using three parallel actions: proportional, integral and derivative. Proportional action reacts to the present error, integral action removes offset, and derivative action responds to the error's slope. The same three-term structure runs motor drives, furnace temperature loops, drone attitude control and flow control in process plants. This chapter writes the parallel PID transfer function, defines each gain with its unit, and shows how P, PI, PD and PID change first-order and second-order responses. Tuning rules follow in 5.3.
prereq: You need Unit 2 steady-state error and second-order damping, plus the Routh test from Unit 3; tuning rules are in 5.3.

blocks.text: Let e(t)=r(t)−y(t) be the error, with r(t) the set point and y(t) the measured output. The parallel PID controller is defined by its transfer function:

blocks.where: C(s) is the controller transfer function; K<sub>p</sub> is the proportional gain (dimensionless in normalized units); K<sub>i</sub> is the integral gain (s<sup>−1</sup>); K<sub>d</sub> is the derivative gain (s); s is the Laplace variable.

blocks.text: In the time domain the control signal is u(t)=K<sub>p</sub>e(t)+K<sub>i</sub>∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>e(τ)dτ+K<sub>d</sub>de/dt. The first term looks only at the present error. The second term adds area under the error, so a small remaining offset keeps pushing the control until the offset disappears. The third term uses the slope, so it pushes early when the error is changing quickly.

items: P: gain now. Larger K<sub>p</sub> speeds the loop and reduces offset, but too large K<sub>p</sub> causes overshoot.
I: memory of accumulated error. Removes step offset; adds phase lag and can slow or oscillate.
D: slope. Adds damping and speed, but amplifies sensor noise.

sections.h3: Effect on first- and second-order plants

blocks.text: For a first-order plant G(s)=K/(τs+1) with unity feedback and P control only, the closed-loop time constant becomes τ/(1+KK<sub>p</sub>). Define K as the plant gain (dimensionless here), τ as the open-loop time constant in seconds, and K<sub>p</sub> as the proportional gain. A larger K<sub>p</sub> gives a faster rise and smaller step error. The step error is 1/(1+KK<sub>p</sub>); it falls but never reaches zero. Adding I makes the loop type 1, so the step error becomes zero. The cost is a slower approach and possible overshoot.

For the second-order plant G(s)=ω<sub>n</sub>²/[s(s+2ζω<sub>n</sub>)] with unity feedback, proportional gain K<sub>p</sub> gives the characteristic equation s²+2ζω<sub>n</sub>s+K<sub>p</sub>ω<sub>n</sub>²=0. Here ζ is the damping ratio (dimensionless) and ω<sub>n</sub> is the natural frequency in rad/s. Compare with s²+2ζ<sub>eff</sub>ω<sub>n,eff</sub>s+ω<sub>n,eff</sub>²=0. Then ω<sub>n,eff</sub>=ω<sub>n</sub>√K<sub>p</sub> and ζ<sub>eff</sub>=ζ/√K<sub>p</sub>. So P raises speed but lowers damping. PD control C(s)=K<sub>p</sub>+K<sub>d</sub>s adds a zero and changes the s coefficient to 2ζω<sub>n</sub>+K<sub>d</sub>ω<sub>n</sub>², so ζ<sub>eff</sub> increases; PD adds damping. PID keeps the integral for zero offset and uses derivative for damping.

PI control raises the system type by one. A type 1 plant such as the one in the worked example becomes type 2, so a unit ramp gives zero steady-state error. A type 0 plant becomes type 1: step error becomes zero, but ramp error is finite. Some syllabi call PID the three-term controller.

The parallel form above is the easiest to add branch by branch. The standard form is C(s)=K<sub>p</sub>(1+1/(T<sub>i</sub>s)+T<sub>d</sub>s). Here T<sub>i</sub>=K<sub>p</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> is the integral time in seconds, and T<sub>d</sub>=K<sub>d</sub>/K<sub>p</sub> is the derivative time in seconds. K<sub>p</sub> still sets the overall gain.

The series form, also called the interacting form, is C(s)=K<sub>c</sub>(1+1/(T<sub>i</sub>s))(1+T<sub>d</sub>s). K<sub>c</sub> is the series gain. The two forms give the same input-output behaviour only for particular gain combinations. Before replacing one controller with another, compare coefficients; do not set K<sub>d</sub>=T<sub>d</sub> unless K<sub>p</sub>=1.

Reading a loop: P sets speed, I removes offset, D adds damping. In frequency terms, I adds phase lag at low frequency, and D adds phase lead near the loop band. Real derivative action is noisy, so industrial PID adds a filter; real integral action needs anti-windup. Those practical limits are separate from the linear transfer function.

figure.caption: The error feeds Kp, Ki/s and Kd s branches; their outputs add to form the plant input. The integral branch carries memory, while the derivative branch responds to the slope.

spec.aria: An error signal feeds three parallel branches with gains Kp, Ki/s and Kd s, and the three branch outputs add before the plant.

examples.question: For G(s)=1/[s(s+2)] with unity feedback, (a) find K<sub>p</sub> so the closed-loop damping ratio ζ=0.5; (b) with K<sub>p</sub>=4 and PI integral gain K<sub>i</sub>=1 s<sup>−1</sup>, find the steady-state error to a unit ramp.
steps: (a) With P control, the closed-loop characteristic equation is 1+K<sub>p</sub>G(s)=0. Put G(s)=1/[s(s+2)]: 1+K<sub>p</sub>/[s(s+2)]=0, so s²+2s+K<sub>p</sub>=0.
Compare s²+2s+K<sub>p</sub>=0 with s²+2ζω<sub>n</sub>s+ω<sub>n</sub>²=0. The s coefficient gives 2ζω<sub>n</sub>=2, so ζω<sub>n</sub>=1. With ζ=0.5, ω<sub>n</sub>=1/0.5=2 rad/s.
Then K<sub>p</sub>=ω<sub>n</sub>²=2²=4. The proportional gain is dimensionless.
(b) The PI controller is C(s)=K<sub>p</sub>+K<sub>i</sub>/s=4+1/s=(4s+1)/s. The open loop is L(s)=C(s)G(s)=(4s+1)/[s²(s+2)].
L(s) has two poles at s=0, so the open loop is type 2. For a unit ramp R(s)=1/s², the velocity error constant is K<sub>v</sub>=lim<sub>s→0</sub>sL(s)=∞.
examples.answer: K<sub>p</sub>=4, ω<sub>n</sub>=2 rad/s, and the unit-ramp steady-state error with K<sub>p</sub>=4 and K<sub>i</sub>=1 s<sup>−1</sup> is 0.
examples.check:
zeta = 0.5
a = 2.0
wn = a / (2 * zeta)
Kp = wn ** 2
Kv = float('inf')
ess = 1.0 / Kv
print(Kp)
print(wn)
print(ess)

traps: Mixing parallel and series gains: in C(s)=K<sub>p</sub>+K<sub>i</sub>/s+K<sub>d</sub>s, K<sub>d</sub> has unit seconds; in standard form T<sub>d</sub>=K<sub>d</sub>/K<sub>p</sub> also has unit seconds, but K<sub>d</sub>=T<sub>d</sub> only when K<sub>p</sub>=1.
Derivative action amplifies high-frequency sensor noise. A large K<sub>d</sub> can saturate the actuator even when the true error is smooth.
Integral action winds up during actuator saturation: the error stays nonzero, the integral keeps growing, and the response overshoots when the actuator recovers.
PI raises system type by one. For a type 0 plant it removes step error but leaves a finite ramp error; it does not force ramp error to zero.
P alone leaves offset in a first-order loop. Increasing K<sub>p</sub> reduces offset but never removes it, and too large K<sub>p</sub> lowers damping and causes oscillation.

quiz.q: Write the parallel PID transfer function and give the unit of each gain.
quiz.a: C(s)=K<sub>p</sub>+K<sub>i</sub>/s+K<sub>d</sub>s. K<sub>p</sub> is dimensionless in normalized units, K<sub>i</sub> has unit s<sup>−1</sup>, and K<sub>d</sub> has unit s.

quiz.q: Why does derivative action act like an anticipatory term?
quiz.a: It uses the slope de/dt. If the error is changing quickly, the derivative branch produces a large correction before the error becomes large, so it adds damping and reduces overshoot.

quiz.q: For G(s)=1/[s(s+4)] with unity feedback and P control, find K<sub>p</sub> for closed-loop damping ratio ζ=0.6.
quiz.a: Characteristic equation: s²+4s+K<sub>p</sub>=0. Compare with s²+2ζω<sub>n</sub>s+ω<sub>n</sub>²=0. 2ζω<sub>n</sub>=4, so ω<sub>n</sub>=4/(2×0.6)=3.333 rad/s. K<sub>p</sub>=ω<sub>n</sub>²=11.11.

quiz.q: A type 0 plant G(s)=2/(s+1) has PI controller C(s)=9+2/s in unity feedback. Find the steady-state error to a unit ramp.
quiz.a: L(s)=C(s)G(s)=(18s+4)/[s(s+1)]. The loop is type 1. K<sub>v</sub>=lim<sub>s→0</sub>sL(s)=lim (18s+4)/(s+1)=4. e<sub>ss</sub>=1/K<sub>v</sub>=0.25.

quiz.q: Why does adding PD control to the second-order plant increase damping?
quiz.a: PD adds the zero from K<sub>p</sub>+K<sub>d</sub>s. The characteristic equation becomes s²+(2ζω<sub>n</sub>+K<sub>d</sub>ω<sub>n</sub>²)s+K<sub>p</sub>ω<sub>n</sub>²=0. The s coefficient rises, so ζ<sub>eff</sub>=(ζ+K<sub>d</sub>ω<sub>n</sub>/2)/√K<sub>p</sub> increases for fixed K<sub>p</sub>.

quiz.q: A type 0 plant is controlled by PI. What happens to step error and ramp error?
quiz.a: PI raises the type from 0 to 1. Step error becomes zero because the loop is type 1. Ramp error becomes finite, e<sub>ss</sub>=1/K<sub>v</sub>, not zero.

quiz.q: Name the standard and series PID forms and define T<sub>i</sub> and T<sub>d</sub>.
quiz.a: Standard form: C(s)=K<sub>p</sub>(1+1/(T<sub>i</sub>s)+T<sub>d</sub>s). Series form: C(s)=K<sub>c</sub>(1+1/(T<sub>i</sub>s))(1+T<sub>d</sub>s). T<sub>i</sub>=K<sub>p</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> is integral time in seconds; T<sub>d</sub>=K<sub>d</sub>/K<sub>p</sub> is derivative time in seconds.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial PID adds anti-windup, derivative filtering, bumpless transfer between manual and automatic, and autotuning. Model predictive control uses a plant model to optimize future inputs and is common where PID reaches its limits. Research directions include fractional-order PID, event-triggered PID and data-driven tuning. Search for anti-windup, derivative filter, relay autotuning and model predictive control.
